source_refs.note: Book p. 19-23: 1.9 Transformation of Graphs of Functions: shifting and scaling, Figures 1.14-1.18, Examples 13-14

blocks.text: Graphs of functions can be transformed in various ways to obtain new graphs from basic functions. These transformations include reflection, rotation, stretching, compression and shifting, and are applied to represent changes in functions in algebraic, graphical and real-life contexts. One of the most important applications of these transformations is in computer graphics, where they are used to model, manipulate and animate images and shapes. However, in this section, we shall focus only on three fundamental transformations: horizontal shift, vertical shift and scaling, which are most commonly used in the graphical analysis of functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A transformation takes the graph of a function you already know, such as \(y = x^{2}\), \(y = \sqrt{x}\), \(y = |x|\), \(y = \ln x\) or \(y = 3^{x}\), and moves or reshapes it. You do not plot the new graph from nothing: you take the old graph and slide it, or pull it, or squeeze it.
Two questions decide everything:
1. Is the change made to the input \(x\) (inside the function) or to the output \(y\) (outside the function)? Inside changes act horizontally, outside changes act vertically.
2. Is it an addition/subtraction (a shift) or a multiplication (a scaling)?
Keep these two questions in mind through the whole section.
(i) Shifting of Graphs
Shifting of graphs refers to the movement of a graph from its original position without changing its shape or size. In shifting, the graph is translated either horizontally or vertically.

In mathematical modeling, shifting is used to represent changes in a function due to variations in input or output values. It allows the same basic function to describe different situations by adjusting its position on the coordinate plane.
Horizontal Shift
A graph of the function \(y = f(x)\) is shifted horizontally when the input variable \(x\) is changed to \(x - h\). The resulting graph is represented by the function:

blocks.text_alt: y equals f of x minus h

items: If \(h > 0\): shift \(h\) units to the right
If \(h < 0\): shift \(|h|\) units to the left

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \(x - h\) move the graph to the RIGHT when \(h > 0\)? Take a point \((a, f(a))\) on the old graph. The new function \(y = f(x - h)\) gives the same height \(f(a)\) when \(x - h = a\), that is when \(x = a + h\). So every height of the old graph now appears \(h\) units further right.
Example: \(y = x^{2}\) has its lowest point at \(x = 0\). For \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\) the bracket is zero when \(x = 2\), so the lowest point moves to \(x = 2\): two units to the right, although a minus sign is written.
In the same way \(y = f(x + 3) = f(x - (-3))\) has \(h = -3\) and moves 3 units to the left.
Vertical Shift
A graph of the function \(y = f(x)\) is shifted vertically when the output variable \(y\) is changed to \(y - k\). The resulting graph is represented by the function:

blocks.text_alt: y equals f of x plus k

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Changing \(y\) to \(y - k\) in \(y = f(x)\) gives \(y - k = f(x)\), which is the same as \(y = f(x) + k\). Here the sign works the natural way: \(+k\) adds \(k\) to every output, so every point goes \(k\) units up; \(-k\) brings every point down.
A vertical shift is an outside change (it acts on \(y\)); a horizontal shift is an inside change (it acts on \(x\)). Outside changes behave as they look; inside changes behave the opposite way.

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: Draw the graph of the function \(y = (x - 2)^{2} - 2\) and observe how it can be obtained from the graph of \(y = x^{2}\).
For better understanding of horizontal and vertical shifts, we consider the function: \(y = x^{2}\). This equation represents a parabola with vertex at \((0, 0)\), as shown in Figure 1.14.

Next, we consider the function \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\). This also represents a parabola with vertex at \((2, 0)\). Its graph can be seen in Figure 1.15. Note that the graph in Figure 1.15 can be obtained directly from the graph in Figure 1.14 by shifting it 2 units horizontally to the right.

Now, consider another function \(y = x^{2} - 2\). This equation also represents a parabola with vertex at \((0, -2)\). Its graph is shown in Figure 1.16. Note that this graph can be obtained directly from the graph in Figure 1.14 by shifting it 2 units downward.

blocks.alt: Upward parabola y = x squared with its vertex at the origin, drawn for x from -3 to 3.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.14: y = x², vertex (0, 0) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Upward parabola y = (x - 2) squared with vertex (2, 0) on the x-axis and y-intercept (0, 4).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.15: y = (x − 2)², vertex (2, 0) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Upward parabola y = x squared minus 2 with vertex (0, -2), cutting the x-axis at minus root 2 and root 2.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.16: y = x² − 2, vertex (0, −2) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)
Our table: the same x-values on the three graphs (not printed in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the table down the columns. The column \((x-2)^{2}\) repeats the values of \(x^{2}\), but 2 rows later: the value 0 that \(x^{2}\) has at \(x = 0\) appears at \(x = 2\). That is the shift to the right.
The column \(x^{2} - 2\) is the column \(x^{2}\) with 2 taken away from every entry: the same \(x\), each \(y\) two less. That is the shift downward.
Challenge answer: \(y = (x-2)^{2} - 2\) is \(y = x^{2}\) shifted 2 units right (Figure 1.15) and then 2 units down. Its vertex is \((2, -2)\), it cuts the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 2)\) because \((0-2)^{2} - 2 = 2\), and it cuts the \(x\)-axis where \((x-2)^{2} = 2\), that is at \(x = 2 \pm \sqrt{2}\).
General Formula for Vertical and Horizontal Shift
If both horizontal and vertical shifts are applied together to the function \(y = f(x)\), then the general form of the transformed function is given by:

blocks.text_alt: y equals f of x minus h, plus k

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The point \((0, 0)\) of \(y = x^{2}\) goes to \((h, k)\) in \(y = (x - h)^{2} + k\). This is why the vertex form of a parabola, \(y = a(x - h)^{2} + k\), shows the vertex \((h, k)\) directly.
Every point moves the same way: \((x, y) \to (x + h,\ y + k)\).
Two shifts can be done in either order: a shift right followed by a shift down gives the same graph as a shift down followed by a shift right.
(ii) Scaling of Graphs

Scaling of graphs refers to the stretching or compression of a graph without changing its general shape. In scaling, the graph is enlarged or reduced either in the vertical direction or in the horizontal direction.
Scaling helps in understanding how a function changes when its input or output values are multiplied by a positive constant factor.
Vertical Scaling
If a function \(y = f(x)\) is multiplied by a positive constant \(a\), then the new function: \(y = af(x),\ a > 0\) represents a vertical scaling of the graph of \(y = f(x)\).

blocks.text_alt: y equals a times f of x, a greater than 0

items: If \(a > 1\), then the graph is stretched vertically by factor \(a\).
If \(0 < a < 1\), then the graph is compressed vertically by factor \(\frac{1}{a} > 1\).
Only the \(y\)-values of the graph change, while \(x\)-values remain unchanged.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Each point \((x, y)\) goes to \((x, ay)\): its distance from the \(x\)-axis is multiplied by \(a\). Points on the \(x\)-axis (where \(y = 0\)) do not move at all.
For \(y = 2x^{2}\): the point \((1, 1)\) of \(y = x^{2}\) becomes \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 4)\) becomes \((2, 8)\): a taller, narrower-looking parabola.
For \(y = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}\): \((2, 4)\) becomes \((2, 2)\): a flatter parabola. Here \(a = \frac{1}{2}\) and the compression factor is \(\frac{1}{a} = 2\).
Horizontal Scaling
If a function \(y = f(x)\) is transformed to: \(y = f(ax),\ a > 0\) then, it represents a horizontal scaling of the graph of \(y = f(x)\).

blocks.text_alt: y equals f of a x, a greater than 0

items: If \(a > 1\), then the graph is compressed horizontally by a factor \(a\)
If \(0 < a < 1\), then the graph is stretched horizontally by a factor \(\frac{1}{a} > 1\).
Only the \(x\)-values of the graph change, while \(y\)-values remain unchanged

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Again an inside change works the opposite way to how it looks. In \(y = f(3x)\) the function reaches the value \(f(6)\) already at \(x = 2\), because \(3 \times 2 = 6\). Every point \((x, y)\) moves to \(\left(\frac{x}{a}, y\right)\): its distance from the \(y\)-axis is divided by \(a\).
So multiplying \(x\) by 3 squeezes the graph towards the \(y\)-axis (compression by 3), and multiplying \(x\) by \(\frac{1}{3}\) (that is, using \(\frac{x}{3}\)) pulls it away (stretch by 3). Points on the \(y\)-axis do not move.

blocks.title: Important Note
blocks.text:
If \(a < 0\), scaling is not purely stretching or compression. It results in:
reflection along the \(x\)-axis in \(y = af(x)\)
reflection along the \(y\)-axis in \(y = f(ax)\)
Therefore, in this section we consider only \(a > 0\) to focus on scaling alone.
For better understanding of scaling, we consider the following functions: \(y = \frac{1}{50}(x - 2)^{2}\) and \(y = (3x - 2)^{2}\).

The graph of \(y = \frac{1}{50}(x - 2)^{2}\) is shown in Figure 1.17 which can be obtained from the graph of \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\) (Figure 1.15) using a vertical compression by factor of 50. Similarly, the graph of \(y = (3x - 2)^{2}\) can be obtained from the graph of \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\) by a horizontal compress, that is, by a factor of 3 (see Figure 1.18).

blocks.alt: Very wide upward parabola y = (1/50)(x - 2) squared with vertex (2, 0), drawn for x from -12 to 16, rising only to 3.92 at both ends.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.17: y = (1/50)(x − 2)² (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Narrow upward parabola y = (3x - 2) squared through (0, 4) with vertex (2/3, 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.18: y = (3x − 2)² (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check Figure 1.17 with one point: \(y = (x-2)^{2}\) is 196 at \(x = 16\); dividing by 50 gives \(3.92\), so the curve is still below 4 at \(x = 16\). The vertex \((2, 0)\) does not move (its \(y\) is 0). That is why the parabola looks almost flat.
Check Figure 1.18: with \(f(x) = (x - 2)^{2}\), we have \(f(3x) = (3x - 2)^{2}\). The vertex \((2, 0)\) moves to \(\left(\frac{2}{3}, 0\right)\) (its \(x\) divided by 3), while the point \((0, 4)\) on the \(y\)-axis stays where it is.
Be careful: \((3x - 2)^{2}\) is NOT \(y = x^{2}\) compressed and then shifted 2 to the right; that would be \((3(x-2))^{2} = (3x-6)^{2}\). The order of transformations changes the answer.
General Formula for Scaling of Graphs
If a function \(y = f(x)\) is transformed to \(y = a\,f(bx),\ a > 0,\ b > 0\) then it represents both vertical and horizontal scaling of the graph of \(y = f(x)\).

blocks.text_alt: y equals a times f of b x, a and b greater than 0

blocks.text: If \(a > 1\), the graph is stretched vertically by factor \(a\). If \(0 < a < 1\), the graph is compressed vertically by factor \(\frac{1}{a}\). On the other hand, if \(b > 1\), the graph is compressed horizontally by factor \(b\) and if \(0 < b < 1\), the graph is stretched horizontally by factor \(\frac{1}{b}\).

blocks.caption: Our summary of the four transformations (point (x, y) of y = f(x) moves to)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to apply several transformations in a given order (Examples 13 and 14 and Exercise 1.3):
1. Write the function you have now and give it a name.
2. For a horizontal change (shift or scaling), replace every \(x\) in the current function: \(x \to x - h\) or \(x \to bx\).
3. For a vertical change, work on the whole current function: multiply all of it by \(a\), or add \(k\) to it.
4. Name the result and use it for the next step. Never go back to the original function in the middle.

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem: Let \(f(x) = \ln(x^{2} + 1)\). Find the function obtained after: (i) a vertical stretch by factor 2 (ii) then a shift 1 unit to the left.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \ln(x^{2} + 1)\).
To find: the function after (i) a vertical stretch by factor 2 and then (ii) a shift of 1 unit to the left.
Method: for (i) use vertical scaling \(y = af(x)\); for (ii) use the horizontal shift \(y = g(x - h)\) on the new function \(g\). The order is given, so step (ii) acts on the result of step (i).

Step (i): vertical stretch by factor 2
\[y = af(x),\quad a = 2\]
\[y = 2\ln(x^{2} + 1)\]
Why: a vertical stretch multiplies every output by \(a = 2\); the input \(x\) is not touched, so the whole function \(\ln(x^{2}+1)\) is multiplied by 2.

Name the new function
\[g(x) = 2\ln(x^{2} + 1)\]
Why: the next transformation acts on this function, not on the original \(f\).

Step (ii): shift 1 unit to the left
\[y = g(x - h),\quad h = -1\]
\[y = g(x - (-1)) = g(x + 1)\]
Why: in \(y = g(x - h)\), \(h > 0\) moves the graph right and \(h < 0\) moves it left; 1 unit left means \(h = -1\).

Check:
The lowest point of \(f\) is \((0, 0)\), since \(\ln 1 = 0\). The stretch keeps it at \((0, 0)\) and the shift left moves it to \((-1, 0)\).
\[2\ln((-1)^{2} - 2 + 2) = 2\ln 1 = 0\]
The answer gives 0 at \(x = -1\), as expected.

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem: Let \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x+1}\). Find the function obtained after applying all the following transformations with the given order: (i) vertical stretch by 2 (ii) horizontal stretch by 3 (iii) shift 2 units to the right (iv) shift 1 unit downward
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x+1}\).
To find: the function after the four transformations, applied in the given order.
Method: one formula for each step: (i) \(y = af(x)\) with \(a = 2\); (ii) \(y = g(bx)\) with \(b = \frac{1}{3}\); (iii) \(y = s(x - h)\) with \(h = 2\); (iv) \(y = t(x) + k\) with \(k = -1\). Each step acts on the function produced by the step before it.

(i) Vertical stretch by 2
\[y = 2\cdot\dfrac{x}{x+1}\]
\[= \dfrac{2x}{x+1}\]
We set \(g(x) = \frac{2x}{x+1}\).
Why: \(y = af(x)\) with \(a = 2\) doubles every output.

(ii) Horizontal stretch by 3
\[y = g(bx),\quad b = \tfrac{1}{3}\]
\[y = g\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{2\cdot\frac{x}{3}}{\frac{x}{3} + 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{2x}{x + 3}\]
Let \(s(x) = \frac{2x}{x+3}\).
Why: in \(y = g(bx)\), \(0 < b < 1\) stretches horizontally by \(\frac{1}{b}\); a stretch by 3 needs \(\frac{1}{b} = 3\), so \(b = \frac{1}{3}\). Multiplying top and bottom by 3 clears the small fractions.

(iii) Shift 2 units to the right
The book prints: \(y = (x - h)\), where \(h = 2\). The function name \(s\) is missing; the formula is \(y = s(x - h)\) (see the Book correction below).
\[y = s(x - 2)\]
\[= \dfrac{2(x - 2)}{(x - 2) + 3}\]
\[= \dfrac{2x - 4}{x + 1}\]
Let \(t(x) = \frac{2x - 4}{x + 1}\).
Why: a shift right by \(h = 2\) replaces every \(x\) in \(s\) by \(x - 2\); in the denominator \(-2 + 3 = 1\).

(iv) Shift 1 unit downward
\[y = t(x) + k,\quad k = -1\]
\[y = \dfrac{2x - 4}{x + 1} - 1\]
\[= \dfrac{2x - 4 - (x + 1)}{x + 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{x - 5}{x + 1}\]
Why: moving down 1 subtracts 1 from every output; writing 1 as \(\frac{x+1}{x+1}\) gives one fraction.

Check:
Follow the point \(\left(1, \frac{1}{2}\right)\) of \(f\): (i) \((1, 1)\); (ii) \((3, 1)\); (iii) \((5, 1)\); (iv) \((5, 0)\).
\[\dfrac{5 - 5}{5 + 1} = 0\]
The answer passes through \((5, 0)\). Also the asymptote \(x = -1\) of \(f\) goes to \(x = -3\) in (ii) and back to \(x = -1\) in (iii), matching the denominator \(x + 1\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 14 (iii) the book prints \(y = (x - h)\), where \(h = 2\). The function letter is missing: it should be \(y = s(x - h)\), the function \(s(x) = \frac{2x}{x+3}\) from step (ii) shifted 2 units right. The book's next line, \(y = s(x - 2)\), is correct, and so is its result \(\frac{2x - 4}{x + 1}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(y = f(x - h)\): shift right by \(h\) (\(h > 0\)) or left by \(|h|\) (\(h < 0\)).
\(y = f(x) + k\): shift up by \(k\) (\(k > 0\)) or down by \(|k|\) (\(k < 0\)).
\(y = af(x)\), \(a > 0\): vertical stretch by \(a\) if \(a > 1\); vertical compression by \(\frac{1}{a}\) if \(0 < a < 1\). Only \(y\)-values change.
\(y = f(bx)\), \(b > 0\): horizontal compression by \(b\) if \(b > 1\); horizontal stretch by \(\frac{1}{b}\) if \(0 < b < 1\). Only \(x\)-values change.
Inside changes (on x) act horizontally and the opposite way to how they look; outside changes (on y) act vertically and the way they look.
Several transformations: apply them one at a time in the given order, each on the newest function.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Moving \(y = (x - 2)^{2}\) to the LEFT because of the minus sign. The minus moves it 2 units to the right.
Calling \(y = f(3x)\) a stretch. Multiplying \(x\) by 3 compresses the graph horizontally by 3; a horizontal stretch by 3 is \(y = f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\).
Shifting only one \(x\). In \(y = s(x - 2)\) every \(x\) of \(s\) must be replaced, in the numerator and in the denominator.
Ignoring the order. A vertical scaling done after a vertical shift scales the shift too: \(\frac{1}{2}(f(x) - 6) = \frac{1}{2}f(x) - 3\), not \(\frac{1}{2}f(x) - 6\).
